title: Gmail for event planners on Mac: templates, scheduled sends and Lazur for RSVPs
metaTitle: Gmail for Event Planners on Mac: Templates, Scheduling, RSVPs

intro: Gmail for event planners on Mac runs in your browser, and it handles most of the inbox work well. Three features do the heavy lifting: templates, scheduled send and filters. This page shows how to set each one up on a Mac, where Gmail's limits sit, and what to ask Lazur when you get stuck.
tldr: Gmail on a Mac runs in your browser. The template, schedule and filter steps below come from Google's computer help pages.
Templates work only on a computer, not in the mobile app. Set them up at your desk.
Gmail allows up to 100 scheduled emails at once. Its sending limit applies after more than 500 emails in a day.
Google Calendar cannot show RSVP status for Outlook guests. Ask them to reply by email and count the answers yourself.
Lazur explains, points and drafts text. You read the draft and press Send.

blocks.text: Most event planners treat Gmail as a job board. Venue holds, caterer quotes, guest replies and load-in times all land in one inbox. The fix is not a new app. It is a short set of templates, a few scheduled sends and some filters. Set those up once and the repeat work shrinks.
Gmail on a Mac: what you are working with

The steps on this page match the browser version of Gmail. Open it in Safari or Chrome, whichever you already use for work. Gmail uses the Command key for most of its shortcuts, so the ⌘ symbol shows up a lot below.

blocks.title: Check the menus first
blocks.text: Google moves menus around from time to time. If a label below does not match your screen, search Settings for the same words. Shortcuts stay off until you turn them on.
Set up Gmail templates for invitations and vendor emails

Templates save the most time for planners. A template is a saved draft you can reuse. Google's help page says templates can be turned on and used only from Gmail on a computer. The mobile app does not offer them. Do the setup at your desk.

items: Open Settings > See all settings.
Select the Advanced tab, then find Templates.
Click Enable, then save the change at the bottom of the page.
Click Compose and write one email you send often.
Click More options, then choose Templates > Save draft as template > Save as new template, and name it.

blocks.text: To send a saved template, open Compose and click More options. Choose Templates > Insert template, then finish the message. Click Send yourself when the message reads right.

blocks.caption: Six starter templates. Adjust the wording for each client.

blocks.text: A template is a starting point, not a final draft. Read each one again before you send. Names, dates and times are where planners make the costly mistakes.

blocks.title: Deleting is permanent
blocks.text: Google's help page says deleting a template cannot be undone. Copy the wording into a note before you delete one you still use.
Send template replies automatically with a filter

A filter can send a template to any message that matches your rules. Use it for replies with one fixed answer, such as parking or dress code questions. Test the search before you save the filter. A broad rule catches mail you did not mean to answer.

items: Click the search box, then click Show search options.
Enter criteria, such as a subject line or a sender address.
Click Create filter.
Check Send template and choose the template.
Click Create filter again to save the rule.

blocks.text: Here is a worked example. Say a venue emails prospective clients with the subject 'Tour request'. Search for subject:(tour request) first. If only tour requests appear, the rule is safe. If your own team threads show up too, narrow the search before you save.
Schedule sends so they land at the right hour

Scheduled send matters most across time zones. Gmail lets you hold up to 100 scheduled emails at once. A scheduled email can go out a few minutes after the set time. Plan for that gap so the message still arrives on time.
On a computer, click Compose and write the email. Click the down arrow next to Send at the bottom left, then click Schedule send. Waiting messages sit in the Scheduled folder in the left panel.

Say your caterer is in Chicago and you work from Los Angeles. You want the email to land at 9:00 a.m. Central. Pick Central when you schedule it. On your screen, that send time reads 7:00 a.m. Pacific. Gmail follows the time zone you chose, so check it before you confirm.

blocks.title: Give deadlines a margin
blocks.text: Do not schedule an RSVP reminder for the exact minute the deadline closes. Sends can slip a few minutes, so schedule it earlier.
Gmail sending limits for bulk event invitations

Gmail limits how much mail you can send. Google's help page says you may hit the limit by sending more than 500 emails in a day. The limit also applies when a single email goes to more than 500 recipients. After you hit it, sending may resume within 1 to 24 hours.
The limit changes how you plan a guest list. Think in batches. The math below assumes one email per guest, and it keeps each day at or under 500.

blocks.caption: Days needed at the daily limit, assuming nothing else goes out that day.

blocks.text: A list in the thousands is a job for a bulk mail tool or your event platform, not a personal inbox. Gmail works best for the replies that follow the invitation.
How often event planners send invitation emails

Two surveys give you a benchmark. Both are old. Eventbrite published its findings in December 2018, from a survey with Emma of hundreds of U.S. event creators. Emma's post on the same survey says it covered nearly 400 event creators. Treat these as a 2018 snapshot, not current habits.

Timing is the first decision. In that survey, 27% started two to three months out, and 26% started one month out. Another 14% waited until about two weeks before the event. The chart leaves out the other options.

The send count is the second decision. Eventbrite reports that 30% of event creators send four to five emails per event. Another 25% send three, and 22% send six or more. Emma's post reports that 43% of event planners send one email a week in the month before the event.
Map those counts to content, not just dates. A simple sequence works for many events. Use it as a starting point, then cut or add emails based on the replies you get.

items: Save the date: date, city and venue, with no ask.
Formal invitation: the RSVP link and the deadline.
Reminder: the deadline and the reply link, again.
Logistics: arrival time, parking and the dress code.

blocks.text: Track RSVPs in Google Calendar and Gmail

RSVP tracking in Google Calendar works for guests who use Google Calendar. Google's help page says you can't check RSVP status for guests who use other calendars, such as Outlook. That gap surprises a lot of planners.

blocks.title: Keep response emails on
blocks.text: Google's help page says turning off guest response emails also stops RSVP statuses from third-party users, such as Outlook.

For Outlook guests, ask for a reply by email, then count the answers yourself. A shared headcount sheet keeps the number in one place. See [Google Sheets for event planners on Mac](/for/event-planners/google-sheets) for how to set that up.
Labels and search for each event

Labels keep each event in one place. Click More in the left panel, then Create new label. Name it with the client and the date, so the labels sort well. Apply the label to each thread from the label icon in the toolbar.

Search does the rest. Use operators to narrow a thread, such as from:, to:, subject: and has:attachment. Type in the top search bar, or press / to jump there. A search like label:summer-gala has:attachment finds every contract for that event in one step.
Gmail keyboard shortcuts on a Mac for faster triage

Shortcuts save the most time when a thread runs long. Google's help page lists ⌘ Enter to send, r to reply, e to archive and / to search. Turn shortcuts on first under Settings > See all settings > Keyboard shortcuts.

blocks.text: The help page does not list a shortcut for scheduling. Use the mouse for the down arrow next to Send. The keys still help with the rest of the work.
A worked week for a 300-guest event
Here is how the pieces fit for one event with 300 guests. On Monday, build the six templates at your desk. Turn on the template setting first, because the mobile app cannot do it.
On Tuesday, send the save the date to all 300 guests in one batch. That stays under the daily limit, so you do not need a second day. Schedule the send for 10:00 a.m. in the guests' main time zone.

On Wednesday, schedule the caterer's deposit reminder for 9:00 a.m. in the caterer's time zone. Set up a filter that answers messages with the subject 'parking' using your parking template. Run the search first, then save the rule.
On Friday, open the RSVP view in Calendar. Count the Outlook replies by hand and update your sheet. Most reminders run on their own once they are scheduled, so the Friday check stays short.
Mistakes that cost event planners time in Gmail

items: Setting up templates on a phone. Templates are desktop only, so the setup happens on a computer.
Scheduling for the exact deadline. Sends can slip a few minutes.
Sending one email to more than 500 people. That hits the limit, and sending resumes later.
Forgetting the time zone. Gmail uses the zone you picked when you scheduled.
Filters that match too much. Run the search first to see what it catches.
Deleting a template by accident. Google says deletion cannot be undone.
Trusting RSVP counts from Outlook guests. Those statuses do not show in Calendar.

blocks.text: If you already hit a sending limit, stop for the day. Keep the unsent list in a note. Google says sending may resume within 1 to 24 hours, so pick up the next batch after that window.
Where Lazur fits in your Gmail routine

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac, and it lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud. It can see the thread in front of you, so you do not have to copy it into a prompt.

items: Where is it? Lazur draws a circle and a label around the control you want.
How do I? Ask Lazur to walk you through it. Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click.
What does this say? Lazur reads the open thread and answers out loud.
Say it, don't type it. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app.
Find out. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and comes back with a summary and a report.

blocks.text: Lazur never clicks for you. It points, explains and types text. You still press Send. A wrong headcount in a venue email is easy to miss, so read it yourself.

Lazur also handles everyday work outside Gmail. Ask for a timer, an Apple Reminders item or a Calendar event. Ask it to open a link or run a web search. The [Gmail page](/apps/gmail) covers the email side in more detail.
Privacy when you ask about guest emails

Guest lists hold personal details. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models.
Keep your own habits tight, too. Close any guest spreadsheet you do not need on screen before you ask a question. Ask about the thread you need, not the whole inbox.
Trying Lazur with your Gmail work on a Mac

Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. A Pro trial starts when you first open the app, and no credit card is needed. Check [pricing](/pricing) for the current plans and what each one includes.
Dictation is unlimited on both paid plans. If you want to test the flow on your own threads, start from the [download page](/download).

blocks.title: Test it on a finished thread
blocks.text: Open a vendor thread you already closed. Ask Lazur to explain it, then check the answer against the thread before you trust it on a live client email.

faq.question: Is there a Gmail app for Mac?
faq.answer: This guide follows the browser version of Gmail. The Google help pages it uses do not describe a separate Mac app. Use Gmail in Safari or Chrome, the same way most planners do.

faq.question: Can I use Gmail templates on my phone?
faq.answer: No. Google's help page says templates can only be turned on and used from Gmail on a computer. Set them up at your desk, then use them from a computer when you send.

faq.question: How many emails can I schedule at once?
faq.answer: Google's scheduling help page says you can have up to 100 scheduled emails at once. Scheduled emails can go out a few minutes after the set time, so plan for that.

faq.question: How many emails can I send in a day?
faq.answer: Google's help page says you may hit the limit by sending more than 500 emails in a day. A single email to more than 500 recipients also hits the limit. Sending may resume within 1 to 24 hours.

faq.question: Can I see RSVPs from Outlook guests in Google Calendar?
faq.answer: Not with the status view. Google's help page says you can't check RSVP status for guests who use other calendars, such as Outlook. Ask them to reply by email and count the answers yourself.

faq.question: Does Lazur send my emails for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It points, guides, explains and types text. You read the draft and press Send.

faq.question: Does Lazur store my guest lists or email text?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: Is Lazur a plugin for Gmail?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for any app. It has no partnerships with any app maker.

faq.question: Is there a trial before I pay?
faq.answer: Yes. A Pro trial starts when you first open the app, and no credit card is needed. Check the pricing page for current plans.
